The Altotiberina Fault is a low-angle normal fault depicted by surface geology (Brozzetti, 1995, Boncio et al., 1998), boreholes (Anelli et al., 1994) and seismic profiles (Barchi et al., 1998) that extends along the inner Umbria region for a length of about 70 km, showing a mean N150Â°E direction, dips ENE to a depth of 12-14 km beneath the Umbria-Marche fold-and-thrust belt, and exhibits offset of about 5 km (Barchi et al., 1999; Boncio et al., 1998 and 2000). The studies on the sedimentary sequence infilling the Sansepolcro basin gives evidence that the extensional tectonic act since Upper Pliocene-Lower Pleistocene (Cattuto et al., 1995; Ambrosetti et al., 1978). Comparison between geological and seismological data confirms the Altotiberina Fault geometry and activity, suggesting its role as an active extensional structure that represents the basal detachment of the west dipping seismogenic normal faults of the Umbria-Marche region (Boncio et al., 1998). The convergent strike between the Altotiberina Fault and its antithetic normal faults is reflected by the rising of the branch line to a depth of 4 km in the Sansepolcro area (Barchi, 2002).
Boncio et al. (2000b) propose that the Altotiberina Fault detachment operates a structural control on the seismogenic layer and that its shallowest hanging wall block is active, generating frequent clustering of microseismicity, seismic swarms and small magnitude earthquakes (even on the base of historical earthquake locations). There are no sufficient data to state if the Altotiberina Fault is also able to produce moderate magnitude earthquake or if it creeps accompanied by microseismicity.
This source corresponds to the Monterchi historical earthquake (26 April 1917, Imax=IX, Me=5.9, CPTI Working Group, 1999). Detailed historical report (Oddone, 1919) describes 1 km-long co-seismic rupture and liquefactions aligned with a N150Â°-striking and ENE-dipping normal fault.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Could the Altotiberina low angle normal fault have a direct seismogenic role or does it mainly creep by means of stable frictional sliding?
2) Is the Altotiberina Fault capable of producing large or even moderate magnitude earthquakes?
3) Could the Altotiberina Fault be seismogenic along discrete segments, both confined by lateral discontinuities and in coincidence of steeper fault plane dips?
4) In correspondence of the historical earthquakes is the seismogenic layer (Altotiberina hanging wall) thick enough to nucleate moderate earthquakes?
5) Could historical earthquakes located close to the Altotiberina Fault be nucleated by the activity of antithetic segments?
6) Are the earthquake-induced surface effects described by Oddone (1919) the evidence of the fault-plane coseismic rupture that reached the surface?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Cattuto at al. (1995)
The Authors, on the basis of geomorphological features, anomalies in the drainage pattern, and on the base of lithological, structural and stratigraphical considerations, hypothesize the sequence of paleogeographical events that gave rise to the present landscape of the Anghiari and Sansepolcro basins. Extensional tectonic movements are supposed to start in the Lower Pleistocene creating a wide lacustrine basin, filled by a thick sequence of fluvio-lacustrine sediments. The extensional tectonic activity continued into the Middle Pleistocene by E-dipping normal faults that tilted westward the fluvio-lacustrine sediments and formed the Anghiari Ridge, splitting into two parts the original depression. As a result the original drainage (NE oriented) of the Sansepolcro Basin deviated southwestward producing the independent Anghiari Basin drained by the Sovara stream. Late landscape modifications were dominated by the Tiber River, forming terraces at various elevations.
Barchi et al. (1998)
The history of the CROP 03 project along with the geophysical results achieved is presented in this paper. Data from NVR seismic, refraction seismic, passive seismic, gravimeter, magnetic and heat flow are described, discussed and presented by means of an interpreted profile crossing NE-SW the entire Central Italy, from Punta Ala to Gabicce village. On this basis, a geodynamic scenario envisages an Apennines domain in which compressive tectonics has acted since the Middle Miocene, whereas is now collapsing. The main deep features of the Tiber Valley area are: a westward dip of a thick Adriatic crust (about 35 km) in-between the Marchean foothills and the Tiber Valley; an antiformal stack of crustal slivers in-between the Valdichiana-Valtiberina; an east-dipping Valtiberina normal fault, which develops along the outer limb of the antiformal crustal stack, traceable at depth till about 13 km beneath the Umbro-Marchean Apennines. The tectonic system consist of a master fault, responsible for the formation of the Tiber Valley half graben, and of a family of antithetic faults resulting in a domino-like structure and connected to the grabens of Gubbio and Gualdo Tadino. The geodynamic meaning of this fault system, in spite of its clear geometry and present kinematics, is open to some question: the position of the master fault, localised in the forelimb of the crustal antiformal stack, would suggest a collapse phenomenon of the orogenic building as the tectonic setting of western domain displays; the low-angle east-dipping normal fault might have reactivated a former back-trust to stretch the crust, when, after the Oligocene, the subduction flipped and the convergence rate became consequently lower than the subduction roll-back.
Boncio et al. (1998)
These workers describe the geometry of the NNW-SSE trending, east-dipping, Altotiberina fault and of some antithetic splays. The work is based on field evidence and on interpretation of two commercial seismic lines, from the Tiber Valley to the Umbria-Marche Apennines, south of the CROP 03 line. The Altotiberina fault exhibits a staircase trajectory, starting as a steep, shallow fault below the Tiber Valley to the W and the becoming an almost flat surface to the E. Its dip angle is low-medium (30Â°-40Â°) below the carbonate formations, at its eastern edge. Detailed microseismic data supplied by the 1991-1994 recordings of the local Umbria seismic network, by a temporary network set up soon after the 29 April 1984 M 5.2 Gubbio earthquake (Haessler et al., 1988) and during May-June 1987 (Deschamps et al., 1989), are also used for understanding the relationships between the Altotiberina fault and regional seismicity. The distribution of seismic activity appears to be controlled by the Altotiberina fault, which separates an active hanging wall block, slipping towards the NE, from an almost aseismic foot wall block. Frequent microearthquakes and moderate size earthquakes are related to the activity of antithetic fault splays, such as the Gubbio fault. The interpretation of two seismic profiles shows an active wedge-shaped rock volume, whose base deepens eastward. The seismicity of the Tiber Valley, of the Gubbio area and of the Umbria Valley is concentrated around 6 km depth and tends to deepen towards the ENE, up to about 12 km beneath the Apennine chain. The authors point out that seismicity tends to concentrate exactly where the main antithetic faults (Gubbio and Colfiorito) intersect the Altotiberina fault, at about 6 km depth. In summary, this seismotectonic study identifies a highly seismic crustal block located east of the westernmost main antithetic faults. This crustal block is characterised by small to moderate earthquakes and by frequent microseismicity mainly clustered in the foot wall of the main antithetic faults, especially near their branch point. A second crustal block, west of the main antithetic faults, has a relatively aseismic behaviour.
Such antithetic faults play a role of release-fault between both blocks and the shallow microseismicity located in their hanging wall is interpreted as the result of adjustment processes due to the collapse.
Bonini (1998)
A geologic-structural study of the plio-pleistocene continental Tiber basin has been carried out allowing to establish the role of strike-slip, compressional and extensional deformations affecting the deposits during the basin evolution.
On the basis of field mapping and structural analysis, the development during Lower-Middle Pliocene of the three branches of the Tiber lake (Upper Tiber basin, Middle Tiber basin and Umbria basin) has been referred to a compressive regime. During Lower Pleistocene the Tiber Basin was controlled by NW-SE trending normal faults cross-cutting obliquely the NNW trending older branches.
The area was further affected by a NE-oriented shortening phase between Lower and Middle Pleistocene. The Pleistocene evolution of this sector has been also investigated by means of analogue modelling experiments, whose results support the hypothesised tectonic progression. A succession of NE to ENE-trending direction of compression or extension led to the reactivation of suitably-oriented pre-existing tectonic structures. The Anghiari-S.Sepolcro depression, northern part of the Upper Tiber basin, is bounded by normal faults that down-throw the Early Pleistocene deposits since the Middle-Late Pleistocene. The S.Sepolcro Fault bounds the northeastern margin of this depression and dips to southwest. The Anghiari fault limits exposures of continental Early Pleistocene deposits to the northeast and dips to northeast. These mesoscopic normal faults indicating a NE-SW direction of the extension, whereas Early and Middle Pleistocene deposits present evidences of a NW-SE-trending direction of compression.
Sani et al. (1998)
Geologic-structural studies were performed in the internal basin of the Northern Apennines. This analysis led to recognise some main compressive event, affecting the continental sedimentary sequences and producing sedimentary unconformities.
A transect crossing the Tiber basin was investigated, too. The Authors relate the development of the whole Tiber basin to a Lower Pliocene shortening phase, produced by the activity of the thrusts bounding the basin, followed by a new compressive phase, which occurred between Lower and Middle Pleistocene. In general, they point out that roughly NW-SE normal faults obliquely overprint the NNW trend of the three main branches, the Upper Tiber basin, the Middle Tiber basin and the Umbria basin. For this reason, they relate these normal faults to a younger phase that affected the basins, developing the Anghiari-Sansepolcro and the Bastardo basins, filled by Lower-Middle Pleistocene deposits.
Barchi et al. (1999)
This work focuses on the results of the analysis of the deep reflection seismic profile CROP 03 and of other commercial seismic lines, both orthogonal and parallel to the upper Tiber valley and to the adjacent Umbrian pre-Apennines.
The subsurface geometry of the Altotiberina fault is presented in a geological section showing WSW-dipping antithetic faults, the most important of which affects the carbonatic anticlines of Gubbio and Assisi. An isobaths map of the Altotiberina fault was reconstruct and shows: a N150Â° strike and ENE dip direction; a steep shallow trajectory up to 4 km and a flat section between 4 and 6 km; its continuity in depth up to 14 km. The different dip angle of the fault is related to the different rheology of the involved fault surface formations. Between Umbertide and Perugia, the Altotiberina fault seems to deepen and shift westward due to the action of a N-S trending structure, as suggested by the isochronous map. Near Umbertide the thickness of continental sedimentary sequence reaches 1400 m. A regional meaning of the Altotiberina fault, 80 km long and 5 km of maximum offset, is confirmed.
Calamita et al. (1999)
On the basis of structural and geomorphological studies, the Authors pointed out the major steps of Plio-Quaternary tectonic and landscape evolution between the Tiber Valley and the Adriatic coast. The Altotiberina fault is interpreted as related to the instability of the orogenic wedge and is considered to be re-activated from Middle Pliocene. Its activity led to the development of the Tiber basin producing local extensional and compressional structures according to its staircase geometry. NE and SW-dipping normal faults affect the Umbria Valley and are antithetic to the Altotiberina fault. The Authors suggest that such faults present an higher activity, compared with the Altotiberina fault, since 0.7 Ma driven by a N10Â°-20Â° extension coupled with the uplift related to the gravitational collapse of the orogenic wedge.
Boncio et al. (2000a)
This work presents a seismotectonic model in the Umbria-Marche Apennines by integrated analysis of geological, geophysical and seismological data. The recent Norcia, Gubbio and Colfiorito earthquakes as well as a major group of microearthquakes are seen to be compatible with a tensional state of stress, characterised by a NE-trending sub-horizontal sigma 3-axis. This stress tensor, which is parallel to the Plio-Quaternary stress field deduced from fault kinematics, may be considered representative of the mean regional present-day state of stress. The nucleation of most damaging earthquakes is assumed to have occurred at the base of the aftershocks volume, close to the intersection between the SW-dipping antithetic normal faults and the main E-dipping Altotiberina fault. The progressive deepening of the seismicity from the westernmost sectors (Gubbio) to the easternmost ones (Norcia) appears to be well related to the Altotiberina fault basal detachment, as imaged by seismic profiles. An almost continuous microseismic activity (M<3) is spread within the hanging wall volume of the Altotiberina fault. The seismic potential of the active faults is expected to be higher in the easternmost seismic zone, where the detachment is deeper.
Boncio et al. (2000b)
One of the aims of this work is to estimate the seismogenic behaviour of the Altotiberina fault, which activity is still debated. The Authors pointed out the lack of data to state a direct seismogenic role of the Altotiberina fault and to understand if it is mainly creeping, possibly coupled with seismic slip along minor structures, or if it is also able to produce moderate-magnitude or even large earthquakes. In their opinion they cannot exclude that such low-angle fault might be seismogenic along discrete and relatively steep segments, also on its shallowest part. The Altotiberina fault belongs to a regional NE dipping low-angle normal fault system (Etrurian Fault System), which extends for about 350 km from north-western Tuscany to southern Umbria. Preliminary considerations suggest that the Etrurian Fault System may play an important role in controlling active extension and related seismicity in entire north-central Italy.
Lavecchia et al. (2000)
This work provides a map of the most relevant seismogenic faults of the Umbria-Marche-Abruzzo Apennine coupled with their parameters. A tentative seismotectonic zonation is presented and shows how its main structure, The E-dipping Altotiberina Fault, controls the distribution of the instrumental and the historical seismicity. The Altotiberina Fault trace, well constrained from Sansepolcro to Perugia, divides a western quasi-aseismic area from an eastern active area. The synthetic and antithetic faults on the Altotiberina Fault hanging wall consent to subdivide zones with different amount of seismicity. The most seismically active zone (intense historic and instrumental seismicity, up to M=6.8) coincide with the area of the w-dipping master faults located in the Altotiberina Fault hanging wall. The Sansepolcro area represents the northward continuity of this active zone and its historical seismicity is supposed to be nucleated not only by the W-dipping but also by E-dipping faults.
Barchi (2002)
By means of seismic reflection profiles, the Author illustrates NNW-SSE trending, SW-dipping normal faults (Umbrian Fault System), extended from Sansepolcro to Norcia, responsible of most of the moderate earthquakes of the region. Seismic profiles reveal that this SW-dipping normal fault seismogenic system is antithetic to the ENE-dipping Altotiberina Fault. It is supposed that the Altotiberina Fault detachment operates a structural control on the seismogenic layer, both deepening from the internal to the external sectors of the Apennines. The Author point out that the Umbrian Fault System is not controlled by a single, major, west dipping thrust. Conversely, different segments of the normal fault system reactivate different thrust faults. A comparison between seismicity, lithology and structures along the Umbrian Fault System is provided, and show a general deepening toward SSE. In the Sansepolcro area, the depth of the intersection between the Altotiberina Fault and the seismogenic Umbrian Fault System rise up to 4 km.
